ut_tower_one.blurb: Tower One is the first wall most parties reach on the way up to the main Hellgate cliffs, in the high country above Snowbird at roughly 8,500 feet. It packs about two dozen routes into a compact face, mostly bolted lines with a few trad climbs, so a small rack is worth bringing along. Grades range from easy 5.6 to 5.12, with the biggest cluster in the 5.10 to 5.11 range, which makes it a good stop for solid intermediate leaders. Routes are long enough that a pair of ropes is handy for lowering or rappelling, and the walk in is short. Expect a lively, popular wall rather than a quiet corner.

ut_sand_dunes.blurb: Sand Dunes is a sandstone wall inside Snow Canyon State Park, a short drive from St. George. It is known for longer outings: many lines run two to five pitches, and the main multi-pitch routes start from a second tier reached by a steep gully. Sport and trad climbs are about evenly split. Most grades sit between 5.7 and 5.10, with a handful of easier lines and a few harder ones near 5.11 and 5.12, so it suits parties wanting moderate adventure climbing. Most routes can be descended on one 60 meter rope. The sandstone is fragile after rain, so give it a couple of days to dry before pulling on holds.

ut_simian_complex_the.blurb: The Simian Complex is a short, steep limestone wall in the Utah Hills, southwest of St. George at about 5,000 feet. The rock is banded orange and gray, and all 23 routes are bolted sport lines to chains. This is a crag for strong climbers: most of the routes fall around 5.12, with a good number at 5.13 and only a few at 5.10 and 5.11. Walls here are brief rather than tall, so expect powerful, steep pitches over endurance outings. A couple of pullouts sit right below the base, making it easy to stop for a session.

ut_jobsite_the.blurb: The Jobsite sits on the north side of Rock Canyon above Provo, and its walls face south. The rock is pale quartzite resting on a dark brown band of tillite. Most of the 23 routes are bolted sport lines, plus a couple of trad climbs, with grades running from easy 5.5 up through 5.13. The left side offers moderate climbing on sharp, irregular rock, while the middle and right sections are steeper and built around large roofs, so the harder routes cluster there. A few lines continue to an upper tier. Route names riff on odd jobs the developers once held, and the crag is a decent choice for newer leaders on its easier left side.

ut_lisa_falls_buttress.blurb: Lisa Falls Buttress stands beside a year-round waterfall in Little Cottonwood Canyon. Most of the 23 routes are low-angle slabs, both bolted and trad, and the grades lean easy, with plenty up to 5.9 and only a few climbs at 5.10 or 5.11. That makes it one of the friendlier places in the canyon for beginners, although a few routes are runout, so check each line's protection before leaving the ground. A hidden section off to the right has a big roof that climbs either tackle or avoid. The face looks south, the moving water cools the air, and many routes catch shade at different times of day.
ut_lisa_falls_buttress.approach: A short, easy path of roughly 200 yards leads up from the road beside the waterfall to the base of the slabs.

ut_east_face_3.blurb: The East Face is one side of Challenge Buttress in Big Cottonwood Canyon, a quartzite cliff on the Wasatch Front's busy canyon road. The terrain is varied, with small outcrops, arêtes and gullies rather than one clean wall. Most of the 23 routes are trad, with some bolted lines and a single top-rope, spanning roughly 5.5 to 5.11. The bulk of the climbing sits between 5.8 and 5.10, so it works well for climbers stepping up from beginner grades who want to place gear. Early sun catches some of the arêtes. The buttress as a whole can get crowded, and you can pick its north, west or east side to suit the weather.
ut_east_face_3.parking_note: Leave the car at the Stairs Gulch pullout, just below the Storm Mountain picnic area, where the creek passes under the road.
ut_east_face_3.approach: From the Stairs Gulch pullout, scramble up the bank southwest of the creek crossing and follow the trail through the trees to a fork. Take the left branch to reach the east side.

ut_kung_fu_theater.blurb: Kung Fu Theater is a sandstone wall in Zion National Park, close to the Mount Carmel tunnel on the east side of the park. The wall faces roughly north and holds plenty of shade, which makes it a popular choice on hot days. Most of the 23 routes are trad, with a few bolted lines, something unusual for Zion. Expect both single-pitch cragging and multi-pitch routes of two to six pitches. Nearly all the climbing is between 5.8 and 5.12, with the biggest group at 5.10 and a solid number at 5.11. The rock is high quality but delicate, and it should never be climbed while wet.

ut_keel_the.blurb: The Keel is a quartz monzonite formation near the mouth of Little Cottonwood Canyon, split by climbers into east, south and west sectors. Despite the name, it does not resemble a boat hull. The roughly two dozen routes are mostly trad, with a couple of sport lines and one aid route, and several are multi-pitch. Grades start with a few easy lines, then concentrate between 5.8 and 5.11, with one climb in the 5.12 range. The walls are broken in places, and the west-facing side picks up good afternoon sun in winter. Parking is in the lower canyon lot, followed by a climbers' trail.

_conflicts.ut_tower_one: Stored rock is quartzite, but the parent area page describes Hellgate Cliffs as white limestone towers: https://mountainproject.com/area/105739780/hellgate-cliffs
